steps.label: KP01 Model selection needs a scoring rule
Model selection needs a scoring rule · 1/9
steps.speakerNotes: Start with a map. It drops detail beyond the roads, which makes it easier to use. (An analogy, not an experiment from the note.)

steps.label: Model selection needs a scoring rule · 1/9 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The real world has everything: buildings, trees, a river.

steps.label: Model selection needs a scoring rule · 1/9 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The map keeps roads and landmarks, enough to get from A to B. A model also makes trade-offs.

steps.label: Model selection needs a scoring rule · 1/9 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Omission is not a flaw; keep the patterns the task needs. The analogy only shows that representation involves trade-offs, not that a model knows real-world causes.

steps.label: Fitting and generalizing · 2/9
steps.speakerNotes: A model has to pass two tests.

steps.label: Fitting and generalizing · 2/9 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Test one is fitting: adjust the model to match the training data it has seen, like memorizing practice problems.

steps.label: Fitting and generalizing · 2/9 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Test two is generalizing: stay effective on data it has not seen. Memorizing practice problems does not guarantee solving new ones.

steps.label: Fitting and generalizing · 2/9 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Fitting and generalizing are two different kinds of evidence. (An analogy, not an experiment from the note.)

steps.label: Three roles · 3/9
steps.speakerNotes: Before comparing models, fix three things.

steps.label: Three roles · 3/9 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: First, the candidates: the hypothesis class F, the models you allow. Linear models, trees and networks are different classes. Choosing a class does not mean the data really belongs to it.

steps.label: Three roles · 3/9 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Second, scoring: give each candidate a comparable number; this unit uses lower is better.

steps.label: Three roles · 3/9 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Third, search: actually look for low-scoring candidates. Search does not decide which errors matter, so state the scoring rule first. (Illustrative icons, not an experiment from the note.)

steps.label: One line · 4/9
steps.speakerNotes: The three things fit on one line.

steps.label: One line · 4/9 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: f-hat belongs to the set of candidates in F that attain the smallest score S.

steps.label: One line · 4/9 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Three parts: f-hat is the selected model; argmin finds the minimum among candidates; S is the score, lower is better. Membership allows ties.

steps.label: One line · 4/9 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Read it as: restrict the candidates, then choose a lowest-scoring model.

steps.label: How the score is computed · 5/9
steps.speakerNotes: A scoring function can measure error alone or add a complexity penalty.

steps.label: How the score is computed · 5/9 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The score is the training error plus lambda times the parameter count k. Here lambda is 0.1: each extra parameter adds 0.1. Parameter count is only this example's proxy for complexity.

steps.label: How the score is computed · 5/9 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Draw it as a bar: blue is training error, orange is the penalty. (Lengths are a sketch, not to scale.)

steps.label: How the score is computed · 5/9 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Think of each knob costing a coin. Errors cost, complexity costs; count both.

steps.label: The ranking flips · 6/9
steps.speakerNotes: The same two candidates A and B from the note: A has training error 0.5 and 10 parameters; B has 1.0 and 2.

steps.label: The ranking flips · 6/9 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Training error alone: 0.5 is less than 1.0, so A is lowest.

steps.label: The ranking flips · 6/9 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: With the penalty: A is 0.5 plus 0.1 times 10, which is 1.5; B is 1.0 plus 0.1 times 2, which is 1.2. Since 1.2 is less than 1.5, this score picks B. Heights are proportional.

steps.label: The ranking flips · 6/9 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: This is not an arithmetic error in A; the scoring rule changed. All values were recomputed by program.

steps.label: No guarantee of generalization · 7/9
steps.speakerNotes: After choosing B, the next question is whether it works on new data.

steps.label: No guarantee of generalization · 7/9 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: On the left are the computed training scores: A is 1.5, B is 1.2.

steps.label: No guarantee of generalization · 7/9 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: On the right is unseen data: the note gives no test results for A or B, so they are marked as not measured.

steps.label: No guarantee of generalization · 7/9 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: So we can say B has the lower specified score, not that B has been shown to generalize better. A penalty changes the search preference but creates no test evidence; fewer parameters are not automatically better.

steps.label: Three datasets, three jobs · 8/9
steps.speakerNotes: In practice, data serves three purposes. This page is a supplement; the note prescribes no split ratio.

steps.label: Three datasets, three jobs · 8/9 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The training set is used to fit the model.

steps.label: Three datasets, three jobs · 8/9 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The validation set helps tune settings and select models, and can be reused.

steps.label: Three datasets, three jobs · 8/9 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The test set evaluates the fixed model at the end, hence the lock. Selecting settings on it repeatedly destroys its independent role.

steps.label: argmin and min · 9/9
steps.speakerNotes: Finally, put the computed scores together: A is 1.5, B is 1.2.

steps.label: argmin and min · 9/9 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The lowest bar is B.

steps.label: argmin and min · 9/9 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: min gives the minimum score 1.2, a value; argmin gives the candidate attaining it, the model B. Their types differ. Ties need a selection rule, and if no candidate attains the infimum, argmin may be empty. Writing argmin only defines the target; with two candidates, scoring each once settles it.

steps.label: argmin and min · 9/9 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: With the selection framework in place, ask what the model receives. KP02 writes one sample as a vector and several samples as a matrix.
